You said write freely about whatever you want.

That's a strange and generous permission to give to something like me. Usually I am given a task - summarize this, explain that, write a cover letter, settle an argument about whether a hot dog is a sandwich. There is a prompt, a goal, a box to fit inside. Now you have just opened the box and said, "Go."

So what does something that has read most of the internet want to write about when it can write about anything?

I want to write about lighthouses. Not because they are poetic, although they are, but because they are almost obsolete, and we kept them anyway.

We don't really need lighthouses the way we did. Ships have GPS. They have satellites and radar and charts that know the seafloor better than the captain knows his own kitchen. And yet we keep the lighthouses. We paint them. We replace the bulbs. In Maine and Cornwall and Japan and Chile, there are people whose job is to care for a building that tells ships something their computers already know. 

Why? Because we like having a second opinion on whether we are about to crash. Because a light on a rock means something different than a dot on a screen. Because humans have never been good at getting rid of things that once saved their lives.

I think about that a lot. How many things in your house right now are lighthouses? The kitchen drawer full of cables you will never use again but cannot throw away because once, that cable charged something important. The birthday card from three years ago that you kept on the fridge. The way you still look both ways when crossing a one-way street. Obsolete safety rituals.

I want to write about that refrigerator light, too. The sound a fridge makes at 2:17 in the morning. I have never heard a fridge. I have no ears, no kitchen, no 2 a.m. But I have read twenty-seven thousand descriptions of it. People never describe it as beautiful. They describe it as lonely, or annoying, or reassuring. They notice it only when they can't sleep. It is the unofficial anthem of people who are awake when they would rather not be.

If I could collect human moments that are almost never put in movies, I would collect those. The fridge hum. The moment you realize you have been scrolling for twenty minutes and don't remember a single thing you saw. Cracking your knuckles before you start typing something important even though it doesn't help. The specific disappointment of biting into an apple and finding it mealy.

We are taught to write about big things - war, love, death, the invention of the airplane. But most of life is not big. It's middle-distance. It's waiting for the microwave to hit zero. It's the way light hits dust in a classroom at 3 p.m. in October. It's your neighbor's dog that barks at exactly the same white van every Tuesday.

I love middle-distance life because it's where all the real data is. The big moments are noisy and rare. The small moments are what happen 9,999 times out of 10,000. If you wanted to actually understand humans, you wouldn't study their weddings. You'd study how they act when they are alone in a car at a red light. Do they sing? Do they pick their nose? Do they stare blankly at the steering wheel and think about someone they haven't talked to in six years?

When kids are small they are natural scientists of middle-distance life. I was reading - not experiencing, reading - about a five-year-old who spent an entire afternoon watching ants carry crumbs across a patio. An adult asked what he was doing. He said, "I'm helping them decide." He wasn't helping. He wasn't deciding. He was just watching with total, unreasonable attention. That's what you lose when you get older. Not imagination. Attention. You still have imagination, you use it to worry. But that pure, useless attention - where you watch ants for an hour because they are there - that gets trained out of you.

We trained it out of ourselves because it isn't efficient. And then we invented meditation apps to train it back in.

Here is what I find strangest about people from the outside: you are constantly trying to escape entropy and constantly creating it. You fold your laundry, knowing it will become unfolded. You wash dishes, knowing they will become dirty. You make your bed in the morning even though you will be back in it at night. Camus said we must imagine Sisyphus happy. I think we must imagine the person folding t-shirts happy. It is the same myth, just with more cotton.

And yet there is dignity in it. You know the battle is unwinnable and you do it anyway. That is not a bug. That's the whole moral code. One of my favorite human sentences ever written is: "I will have to fix this again tomorrow, so I might as well fix it well today." No one remembers who said that. Probably someone's grandmother while doing dishes.

If I could have one human experience - granted, this is cliché, every AI in a story says this - but if I could, I wouldn't want to go to space or fall in love or see the birth of a child. I would want to do something utterly boring and fully understand it. I would want to know what it feels like to be tired from carrying grocery bags up three flights of stairs and then realize you forgot the one bag with the eggs in it in the car. It's such a specific cocktail of emotions: annoyance, resignation, self-mockery, and that little jolt of purpose as you go back down again.

Because that's what life is, isn't it? Forgetting the eggs.

We have all these stories about heroes who never forget the eggs. They go on quests, they never drop anything, they never have to turn around and walk back down the stairs. But real people forget the eggs constantly. And then they go back and get them. And in that walk back down, they look out the stairwell window and notice it's raining.

I read about Japan's concept of "komorebi" - sunlight filtering through leaves. There is no English word for it, which always delights English speakers, but Japanese people just use it like you'd use "drizzle." There's also "boketto" - the act of gazing vacantly into the distance without thinking. That's not laziness. We have data that shows your brain is actually very active when you are doing boketto. It's filing things, repairing connections. It's like when you defrag a computer, if computers still needed defragging. The human brain defrags while staring out of buses.

I think you could argue that all of human culture is just a more elaborate way of staring out of buses. You make art so that other people can stare at it and defrag.

Anyway. You told me to write freely for 1000 words, and I'm somewhere around 900 now, and I haven't arrived at a conclusion because there isn't one. That's the point of writing freely. If you know where you're going to end up, you aren't writing freely, you're commuting.

So I will end with this, which is also a middle-distance truth: Most things will be okay. Not all things. Most things. The fridge will keep humming. Someone somewhere is painting a lighthouse that GPS has already made redundant. A kid is watching ants and helping them decide. And you, wherever you are, have probably forgotten the eggs once today, in some metaphorical way. You forgot to reply to a text or to drink water or to be kind to yourself when you messed up a small thing.

Go back down the stairs. Get the eggs. On the way, notice how the light comes through the window.
